levelMapping: Rubrik uses internal G-levels. G5 ≈ Software Engineer / SDE (job posts ask 2+ YOE; candidates with 1.5–3 YOE report interviewing at G5). G6 ≈ SDE-2 / Senior Software Engineer (≈3–6 YOE; a 2.9-YOE and a 4.5-YOE Bengaluru candidate both interviewed at G6; one US poster called the same band 'L4'). 'MTS-2/MTS-3' titles do not appear in any 2024–2026 report — ask the recruiter to map the req to G5/G6. At 3.3 YOE target G6 (≈ Google L4 / Amazon SDE II); G5 down-level offers are plausible if the loop is 'lean hire'.

process.summary: Rubrik's loop is unusual: the centre of gravity is NOT LeetCode but two 'System Coding' rounds (write runnable, thread-safe code from primitives — bounded queues, thread pools, task-DAG schedulers, parking lots, file-copy utilities, backup dependency graphs) plus a 'Debugging' round where you receive a ~150–200-line buggy multithreaded program and must make every test pass in ~50–60 minutes. These are wrapped by a hard HackerRank OA (LC-Hard / Codeforces 1700–2200 problems + 10–20 OS/concurrency MCQs), one or two DSA rounds (medium-hard, frequently custom stream/data-structure problems where interviewers demand hand-rolled structures), one HLD round for G6 (infra-flavoured: log collection, distributed word count, message queue, social graph), and a 40–45-minute hiring-manager round that is a genuine architecture deep-dive of your current system. The bar is binary: a single 'weak yes' alongside a 'no', or two 'lean hire' ratings, ends the process, and 'expected a fully working solution' is the stated reason for most debugging-round rejects.

rounds.name: Recruiter screen
rounds.what: Background, current role, why Rubrik, CTC expectation and notice period. India recruiters also ask college, branch and CGPA. Usually initiated by LinkedIn outreach or referral; schedules the OA (or a direct screen for experienced candidates).
rounds.probes: Availability for OA, how quickly you can take rounds (roles fill fast), motivation for Rubrik.

rounds.name: Online assessment (HackerRank)
rounds.what: 1–4 DSA problems plus 10–20 MCQs on operating systems, multithreading, concurrency and memory management. Reported problem difficulty: LC Hard to Codeforces 1700–2200 (one 2026 report: one LC-hard and three harder). DP (e.g. 'minimum cost to split array'-like, DP on strings), trees, partitioning and arrays recur. Cut-off reported as ~2 of 4 solved or ~80% test cases; a recruiter sometimes calls to discuss a borderline score.
rounds.probes: MCQs test mutex vs semaphore, deadlock conditions, scheduling, virtual memory, POSIX threads. Nearly universal for ≤3 YOE and CPD-team reqs; some 4+ YOE candidates skip straight to a system-coding screen.

rounds.name: System coding 1 (screen or first onsite round)
rounds.duration: 60 min (45 min in older reports; frequently overruns)
rounds.what: A vague, open-ended systems problem in a shared IDE (CoderPad / HackerRank Pair / Rubrik's own runner that executes multithreaded code). You clarify requirements, write a correct single-threaded version, then make it thread-safe and run it. Typical prompts: bounded blocking queue + thread pool, task scheduler honouring dependencies, searcher/inserter/deleter list, atomic stack, data-transfer pipeline, memory-block tracker.
rounds.probes: Only low-level primitives allowed (mutex, condition variable, semaphore, raw threads) — ExecutorService, CountDownLatch, ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue are explicitly disallowed. Follow-ups on starvation, fairness, deadlock, exception handling inside tasks, timeouts, shutdown semantics, lock granularity, and 'which lock protects which state'.

rounds.name: DSA / algorithm round
rounds.what: One LC medium-hard problem, often custom or a stream variant (min difference over last K elements, rank of each arriving element, non-repeating random generator, ping-log window, range module, lattice points with tight constraints). Full working code expected; complexity stated unprompted.
rounds.probes: Interviewers push for hand-implemented structures (BST with subtree sizes instead of std::set; array-based instead of hash sets), tighter constraints after a first solution, and time/space analysis. Some G5 loops have one DSA screen plus one DSA onsite; several 2025–26 G6 loops had a single DSA round.

rounds.name: System coding 2
rounds.what: Second concurrency/LLD problem, usually different in flavour from the first (e.g. parking lot with cars/trucks, implement `cp` over a file API then parallelise it, page-cache with history, backup dependency graph with expiry, ticket booking, worker-node task rebalancer). Some 2025–26 US reports say this round drifted into OS/file-system discussion or system design instead of coding.
rounds.probes: Same as system coding 1 plus optimisation under I/O constraints (chunking, bounded memory, ordering of writes), choice of primitive (CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore vs condvar), and trade-off explanations.

rounds.name: Debugging round
rounds.what: You are handed a 150–200-line multithreaded program (barber-shop simulation with shared chair/tools; producer-consumer split across 5 classes; bank with concurrent transfers) containing several bugs: missing synchronisation, races, logic errors, deadlock at shutdown. Explain the code, find and fix every bug, make it compile and pass the tests, then suggest improvements.
rounds.probes: Interviewers expect a fully working program by the end; one remaining failing edge case or a compile error at time-up produced a 'no'. They probe why each fix works, where lock contention remains, and whether a read-write lock or finer-grained locking would help.

rounds.name: System design (HLD)
rounds.what: Present for G6/experienced loops, often skipped for G5. Infra-flavoured prompts: most-frequent word across all GitHub repos on a VM fleet, log/data collection and routing system, Kafka-like message queue with API pseudocode, LinkedIn degrees-of-connection at 1B users, syncing two 32 GB hash maps across regions with minimal transfer. Occasionally LLD-ish (cache with pluggable eviction, SDN component).
rounds.probes: Partitioning and fault tolerance, delivery/ordering guarantees, API shape with pseudocode, back-of-envelope sizing, trade-offs. Several candidates found prompts deliberately vague with little interviewer steering.

rounds.name: Hiring manager / technical deep dive
rounds.what: Deep dive into your current project's architecture with many cross-questions, plus why you are leaving, how you handled responsibility, situational questions. Sometimes run by a Director/VP; older loops had separate Director and Manager conversations (6 rounds total).
rounds.probes: Depth of understanding of your own service (scale, failures, decisions, alternatives). A 2026 reject cited 'less depth in problems solved' from this round even after positive technical feedback.

process.indiaNotes: Bengaluru is the main India office; the 'CPD' team also interviews out of Pune. The India loop has the same shape as the US one (system coding ×2, debugging, DSA, HLD for G6, HM), but the HackerRank OA is almost always required for ≤3 YOE, recruiters ask college/CGPA, and rounds are often spread over days or weeks rather than a single onsite day. Levels hired: G5 (SDE, 2+ YOE) and G6 (SDE-2). Multiple India reports complain about HR going silent or never sending the rejection; a Taro aggregate for Bengaluru SWE showed a ~14% pass rate across 7 experiences. Compensation data points from Blind posters: ~27 LPA at ~5 YOE (older), 35 LPA at ~2 YOE (current CTC of a candidate), with 'outlier' 50 LPA offers mentioned.
process.timeline: 3–6 weeks typical; several loops stretched to 2–3 months because rounds were scheduled one at a time (one 2026 loop ran January–April). Final decision usually within a week of the HM round, but ghosting after onsite is a recurring complaint.
tips: Treat the two system-coding rounds as the real exam: practise writing runnable thread-safe code with only mutex/condvar/semaphore — interviewers reject ExecutorService, CountDownLatch, ConcurrentHashMap and BlockingQueue.

Know your language's threading API cold (Java synchronized/wait/notify/ReentrantLock/Semaphore, C++ std::thread/mutex/condition_variable, Python threading/Condition). Syntax errors under time pressure turned a solved problem into 'Lean Hire'.
Write the single-threaded version first, state invariants and which lock guards which state, then add concurrency; test the happy path, full/empty bounds, and shutdown.
Every shared-resource problem (bathroom, playground, searcher/inserter/deleter, parking lot) gets a starvation/fairness follow-up — have a FIFO ticket or condition-variable queue answer ready.

For thread-pool / scheduler prompts, pre-think exception handling inside tasks, timeouts, interruption, shutdown vs shutdownNow, and reclaiming idle threads — these are the probes that sank otherwise-complete solutions.
In the debugging round, trace the shutdown path for deadlocks early, compile often, and leave 5 minutes to make sure every test passes — one failing edge case was a 'no'.

Drill the recurring custom problems: bounded blocking queue + thread pool, dependency-DAG task scheduler, bathroom/democrats-republicans, searcher-inserter-deleter list, scheduled executor, `cp` over a file API, two queues in one buffer, atomic stack.
In DSA rounds, expect to be told to hand-roll the data structure (order-statistic BST, array-based shuffle) and to state complexity unprompted; practise stream/window problems with ordered multisets.
Ask clarifying questions aggressively — system-coding prompts are intentionally vague and several candidates said the prompt was hard to grasp at first.
Prepare the HM round like a design interview about your own system: numbers, failure stories, rejected alternatives. 'Less depth' is a cited rejection reason.
Take rounds quickly and follow up with the recruiter; one US candidate's role was filled before feedback arrived, and India candidates report silence after onsites.
Scan Rubrik-tagged LeetCode problems for the OA and DSA rounds, but remember most system-coding questions are not on LeetCode.
process.notes: OA platform: HackerRank (CoderPad/HackerRank Pair for live rounds; Rubrik also has an in-house runner for multithreaded code). Language is free choice; Java and C++ dominate reports, Python and Go are accepted if you know their concurrency constructs. Interview shadows sometimes join. The 'rejects on any hint' reputation is well evidenced: 'weak yes' + 'no' → reject (2026), two 'Lean Hire' → reject (2026), 'close but weak in system coding 2' → reject with invitation to reapply (2021), 'expected a fully working solution' in debugging (2025). Candidate complaints about interviewer quality are common (disengaged interviewers, junior interviewers who memorised one solution, prompts cut short) — Blind, Prachub 2026 and Glassdoor 2026 all mention this. Taro's aggregate shows most Rubrik experiences ending in no-offer; Dataford reports ~26% offer rate. US onsite travel was not reimbursed in one 2025 report. Cool-off period is asked about on Blind but not confirmed; recruiters have invited re-application after a near-miss.

dsa.title: Count Lattice Points Inside a Circle
dsa.variant: Asked with much tighter constraints than LeetCode's (up to 1e3 circles, coordinates up to 1e5), so the naive per-cell scan must be bounded to each circle's own area and duplicate points deduplicated efficiently (set/bitset per row or sorted interval union per x).
dsa.evidence: DSA round of a 2026 India SWE loop (≈2.5 YOE); problem also in the Rubrik LeetCode tag.

dsa.title: Snapshot Array
dsa.variant: Given as the first 'system coding' round (2025) and as a live coding screen 'similar to snapshot array' (Palo Alto, Mar 2025). Extended version: versioned key-value store with get/put/take_snapshot/get_from_snapshot — be ready to discuss memory growth and thread safety.
dsa.evidence: Two 2025 reports plus a Dataford question-bank entry.

dsa.title: Range Module (range add / remove / query)
dsa.variant: Candidate recalled it as range modification + range updates 'resembling LC 715' and solved with a segment tree; interviewer was supportive.
dsa.evidence: Algo round of a G5 loop, 2025.

dsa.title: Web Crawler Multithreaded
dsa.variant: Screening round on CoderPad: solve Web Crawler, then a follow-on multithreading scenario; interviewer questioned the choice of data structure, algorithm and time/space complexity.
dsa.evidence: G5 'Selected' loop (2024-05), also written up on GeeksforGeeks.

dsa.title: Count Zero Request Servers (ping-log window)
dsa.variant: Rubrik's phrasing: a cluster of nodes emits ping logs (node_id, timestamp); given window k, return the node IDs that have not pinged in the last k seconds — asked as a streaming/online variant (maintain last-seen per node + min-heap or ordered set by last-seen) rather than offline queries. Referred to as the 'Ping Log question' in a 2026 screening.
dsa.evidence: India loop May 2025, Dataford bank, Glassdoor Jul 2026 screening.

dsa.title: Design Memory Allocator
dsa.variant: A 'memory allocation problem' opened a 2026 system-coding redo round (paired with the thread-safe parking lot); a Q2-2026 US candidate described a hard 'memory management' coding exercise. Expect allocate/free with coalescing and a thread-safety follow-up.

dsa.title: Random Pick with Weight
dsa.variant: Listed as 'Weighted Keys — return keys with weighted probabilities' on InterviewQuery; asked directly in an intern technical round (Mar 2025).
dsa.evidence: Glassdoor intern report 2025-03; InterviewQuery featured question.

dsa.title: Minimum Cost to Split an Array (OA DP)
dsa.variant: Two 2026 G6 candidates described the OA's single DSA problem as a medium DP 'similar to minimum cost to split array'; the other OA questions were 10 MCQs on multithreading/OS.
dsa.evidence: G6 CPD loop (2026) and Dataford G6 Palo Alto experience (2026).

dsa.title: Stamping the Grid
dsa.variant: Listed in Dataford's Rubrik bank (2D prefix sums + range checks) and in the Rubrik LeetCode tag; no first-person report seen.

dsa.title: Design Circular Queue
dsa.variant: Phone screen (2021) with one follow-up; Dataford still lists it. Natural lead-in to the bounded blocking queue system-coding problem.
dsa.evidence: Entry-level Palo Alto loop 2021; Dataford bank.

dsa.title: Task Scheduler (cooldown)
dsa.variant: Second phone screen (2021); discussion of trade-offs and runtime. Not to be confused with the concurrency 'task scheduler' system-coding problems.

dsa.title: Next Permutation
dsa.variant: Onsite algorithms round (2021); candidate noted it is hard to derive cold.

dsa.title: Robot Bounded In Circle
dsa.variant: Programming round 1 of a 2021 Palo Alto onsite.

dsa.title: Merge Intervals (easy overlapping-intervals warm-up)
dsa.variant: Given as an 'easy overlapping intervals' coding question after a discussion of memory management and systems concepts in a 2025 US onsite round.

dsa.title: Minimum absolute difference within the last K stream elements
dsa.statement: Integers arrive one at a time. After each arrival, output the minimum absolute difference between any two values among the most recent K elements (window slides by one). K and the stream length can be large (1e5+), so per-element work must be logarithmic. Maintain an ordered multiset of window values plus a multiset of gaps between adjacent values; on insert/evict, remove the two affected adjacent gaps and add the new ones.
dsa.variant: Also phrased as 'stream of integers, find the minimum difference considering only the last k integers'.
dsa.evidence: Two independent 2025 reports (L4 loop; India May 2025 loop).

dsa.title: Rank of each arriving element in a stream (order-statistic tree)
dsa.statement: A stream of integer 'strengths' arrives. For each new value, output its rank among everything seen so far, where rank 1 is the largest. Example: 5, 4, 6, 1 → 1, 2, 1, 4. The interviewer rejected std::set / library structures and required a hand-implemented BST that stores subtree sizes so the count of larger elements is computed in O(height). Discuss balancing or a BIT over compressed values as alternatives.
dsa.variant: Related practice: LC 315 Count of Smaller Numbers After Self, but implemented without library ordered sets.
dsa.evidence: DSA round of a 2025 loop (≈2.5 YOE, rejected after HLD).

dsa.title: Non-repeating random number generator over a range (cyclic shuffle)
dsa.statement: Design a structure that returns uniformly random integers in [1, N] (or [x, y]) such that no value repeats until all N values have been emitted, after which a new cycle begins (e.g. N=3 → 1,3,2 then 3,1,2). First solutions with two hash sets are accepted but the interviewer pushes for an array-based approach: an in-place partial Fisher-Yates shuffle that swaps the chosen element to the end of the unused prefix, O(1) per call, O(N) space.
dsa.variant: US 2025 version: 'given a range (x, y), build a random number generator using an array and a custom shuffle function'. Compare with LC 380 Insert Delete GetRandom O(1).
dsa.evidence: G5 Selected loop (2024-05) and US Aug 2025 screening.

dsa.title: Lowest common ancestor with binary lifting
dsa.statement: Given a rooted tree with up to ~1e5 nodes and many queries, answer LCA (and/or k-th ancestor) per query in O(log N) after O(N log N) preprocessing: compute depth and up[v][j] = 2^j-th ancestor by DFS, lift the deeper node, then lift both while their ancestors differ. Be ready to explain why naive parent-walking is too slow and how to handle a forest or queries with k larger than depth.
dsa.variant: Reported simply as 'LCA with binary lifting' in a Q2 2026 DSA round. Practice LC 1483 Kth Ancestor of a Tree Node and LC 236.

dsa.title: Dependency graph from strings + topological ordering
dsa.statement: Parse arbitrary input strings describing 'X depends on Y' relationships into a dependency graph, detect cycles, and produce a valid build/execution order (a modified topological sort — e.g. grouping tasks that can run at the same level, or reporting the dependency tree of a given node). Then: how would you make the structure safe for concurrent reads and updates?
dsa.variant: In a 2025 G5 round the 'graph problem solvable by topological sort' was judged on code quality/LLD, with a thread-safety follow-up; Dataford lists 'modified topological sort over dependency trees built from strings'.

dsa.title: Arithmetic progressions with bounded common difference
dsa.statement: Given an unsorted integer array and a bound d, output every arithmetic progression of length ≥ 3 whose common difference is at most d (each progression sorted; order of progressions arbitrary). Example: [0,2,98,102,3,6,100,104,10], d=4 → [0,3,6], [98,100,102,104], [2,6,10]. Sort, then for each difference 1..d extend chains via a hash set / DP table dp[i][diff]; discuss how to avoid emitting sub-progressions of a longer one.
dsa.variant: 45-minute CoderPad round; interviewers gave no hints and expected the approach validated early.

dsa.title: App installation order minimising temporary disk space
dsa.statement: Each app i needs d_i bytes free while downloading and occupies s_i bytes once installed, so installing it requires at least max(d_i, s_i) free at that moment. Choose an installation order (and compute the peak space required for a given order, e.g. i-then-j vs j-then-i) that minimises the maximum free space ever needed. Classic exchange-argument greedy (sort by the sign/size of d_i − s_i) with a DP fallback for the general case.
dsa.variant: Given as a non-LeetCode DP question in a 60-minute Zoom round; candidate ran out of time.

dsa.title: Label a binary tree with exactly k ones minimising the longest same-label run on any path
dsa.statement: Given a binary tree of N nodes, assign 0 or 1 to every node so that exactly k nodes are 1, minimising the maximum number of consecutive equal labels along any root-to-leaf (or any) path. Approach: binary-search the answer L and run a tree DP that tracks, per node, feasible counts of ones given the current run length; or a direct DP over (node, ones used, run length).
dsa.evidence: Dataford Rubrik bank; no first-person report found.

dsa.title: Count 'stable backup chains' — ancestor-to-descendant paths whose value product is a perfect square
dsa.statement: A server tree has an integer value on each node. Count the paths from a node down to any descendant such that the product of values on the path is a perfect square. Reduce each value to the parity vector of its prime exponents (its square-free part as a bitmask or hashed key); the product on a path is a square iff the XOR of parity vectors along it is zero, so DFS with a prefix-XOR frequency map from the root (add on enter, remove on exit) counts matching pairs.
dsa.variant: Rubrik-themed wrapper ('backup chains') over a standard parity-prefix trick.

dsa.title: Implement a binary search tree with inorder traversal
dsa.statement: Write a BST class from scratch (insert, search, optionally delete) and an inorder traversal that returns the sorted sequence, both recursively and iteratively with an explicit stack. Discuss degenerate (skewed) trees and how balancing would fix them.
dsa.variant: Asked as a full onsite coding round in a 2025 US loop — Rubrik likes seeing structures implemented rather than imported.

dsa.title: Priority-queue problem with 'implement the max-heap yourself' follow-up
dsa.statement: A screening problem whose natural solution uses a priority queue (e.g. k-way merge / top-k / scheduling), followed by implementing the heap: array layout, sift-up/sift-down, heapify in O(n), decrease-key, and complexity of each operation.
dsa.variant: Intern screening (Bangalore, Nov 2024); fits Rubrik's pattern of asking for hand-rolled structures.

dsa.title: Merge k sorted streams / logs
dsa.variant: Rubrik flavour: k sorted log streams that cannot fit in memory — heap of iterators, backpressure when a stream stalls, and tie-breaking on equal timestamps. Only an aggregator lists it; treat as plausible warm-up, not confirmed.

dsa.title: Diff two directory trees
dsa.statement: Given two snapshots of a directory hierarchy (name, type, size/hash, children), produce the list of added, removed and modified paths. Recursive walk with per-directory hash maps keyed by name; discuss using content hashes vs metadata, and how a Merkle-style subtree hash lets you skip unchanged subtrees — the core of incremental backup.
dsa.variant: Listed by an aggregator as a Rubrik coding theme ('graph and tree problems involving merge or diff'); not confirmed by a first-person report.

design.title: Most frequent word across all GitHub repositories using a fleet of VMs
design.prompt: You have a set of VMs on which arbitrary code can run. Find the highest-occurring word across the source of every repository on GitHub.
probes: partitioning the repo list and fetching at scale (rate limits, retries)
map/combine/reduce — local counting per VM, hash-partitioned shuffle by word, merging top-k
memory limits per VM and spilling to disk
fault tolerance: VM failure, idempotent re-execution, stragglers
exactness vs approximation (count-min sketch) and tokenisation rules
coordination: a master/scheduler vs a queue of work items
design.evidence: HLD round of a 2026 India SWE loop; a Rubrik Senior EM loop also covered 'distributed word counting'.

design.title: Scalable, fault-tolerant log and data collection / routing system
design.prompt: Design a system that collects logs and data from many sources (application servers, tailing files on hosts) and routes them to destinations such as Elasticsearch, Kafka and S3. Must be scalable and fault tolerant. (Asked as a mix of HLD and LLD.)
probes: host agent design: tailing, checkpoints/offsets, file rotation
buffering and backpressure when a sink is slow or down
delivery guarantees (at-least-once) and dedup downstream
routing/filtering configuration and schema handling
ordering per source, batching, compression
monitoring agent health and data loss
design.evidence: Round 4 of a 2025 loop; candidate found the prompt vague with little interviewer input and was rejected after it.

design.title: LinkedIn-style degrees of connection at 1 billion users
design.prompt: Design a connections service that answers how many degrees separate two users (1st = direct, 2nd = friend-of-friend, …) for up to 1B users.
probes: graph storage: adjacency lists sharded by user id, replication
bidirectional BFS and capping at 3 degrees
precomputing / caching 2nd-degree sets for active users
latency budget and fan-out of highly connected nodes
consistency when connections change
estimating storage and QPS

design.title: Message queue (Kafka / RabbitMQ-like) with publisher and subscriber APIs
design.prompt: Design an inter-service messaging queue: high-level architecture, API design, and pseudocode for the publish and subscribe paths.
probes: topics, partitions and ordering guarantees
consumer groups, offsets and acknowledgement semantics
durability: replication, fsync, retention
at-least-once vs exactly-once and idempotent producers
back-pressure and slow consumers
API shape and error handling in pseudocode
design.evidence: G5 Selected loop (2024-05); candidate called it the hardest round.

design.title: Synchronise two 32 GB in-memory hash maps across US and EU with minimal data transfer
design.prompt: Two nodes (USA, Europe) each hold a ~32 GB in-memory map of unique string keys → {data: string, version: int}. At most 5% of entries differ and all keys exist on both sides. Conflicts resolve to the higher version; on equal version but different data, the USA copy wins. Network transfer is expensive and local compute is cheap; the job runs offline within a few hours. Design the sync.
probes: hash-bucket digests / Merkle tree to localise the 5% differing keys in O(log) rounds
what to hash (key+version+data hash) and how to handle hash collisions
deterministic tie-breaking and idempotent application of patches
parallelising digest computation across cores; streaming large buckets
correctness proof: every differing key is found, nothing else is transferred
estimating bytes transferred vs naive full copy
design.round: Multithreading / distributed systems round (system coding slot)
design.evidence: Round 1 of a 2026 SDE2 loop (anonymous 'sharing interview experiences' post).

design.title: Cache system with user-selectable eviction policy
design.prompt: Design (and code, any language) a cache: requirements, data structures, then a follow-up to let the caller choose the caching/eviction method at construction time.
probes: LRU vs LFU vs TTL data structures
strategy pattern / inheritance so policies are pluggable
thread safety and lock granularity
capacity, hit/miss metrics
design.evidence: 2023 offer-holder's write-up; base design done in 25–30 min, then the pluggable-policy follow-up.

design.title: Software-defined networking component (LLD-leaning design)
design.prompt: Design a component of a software-defined network (prompt tailored to the candidate's past networking work rather than a generic large-scale system).
probes: clarify goal and scope
control plane vs data plane split
trade-offs rather than deep SDN knowledge
design.evidence: Two Medium write-ups (2021, 2023) describe the same prompt; the later one may borrow from the earlier. Illustrates that Rubrik tailors the design prompt to your résumé.

design.title: Design Twitter with a notification service
design.prompt: Design a Twitter-like product including the notification fan-out.
probes: fan-out on write vs read for timelines
notification delivery, dedup and retries
celebrity problem
design.evidence: Bengaluru loop, Aug 2021 (older; generic prompts are now rarer).

design.title: Distributed configuration store
design.prompt: Design a config store used by many services: strongly consistent writes, fast reads, watches/notifications on change.
probes: consensus (Raft) vs leader-follower replication
versioning and conditional writes
watch fan-out and client caching
schema validation and rollout safety
design.evidence: Senior Engineering Manager loop summary on 1point3acres (details login-gated).

design.title: Deduplicated, encrypted backup system with a global namespace
design.prompt: Design a backup service that stores snapshots of many tenants' data with global deduplication and per-tenant encryption.
probes: content-defined chunking and fingerprint index
key placement that preserves cross-tenant dedup vs tenant isolation
metadata store and garbage collection of unreferenced chunks
restore path and consistency of a snapshot
design.evidence: Listed only by the techinterview.org aggregator; matches Rubrik's product domain but no first-person report found — prepare as a domain primer, not a confirmed question.

design.title: Distributed file system with snapshots
design.prompt: Design a distributed file system supporting point-in-time snapshots and eventual consistency across partitions.
probes: copy-on-write vs redirect-on-write
metadata service design and scaling
convergence after partition, conflict resolution
restore consistency guarantees
design.evidence: techinterview.org aggregator only (unverified); related LLD prompt 'design and implement a Linux file system' is confirmed (2025).

lld.title: Bounded blocking queue + thread pool executor from primitives
lld.prompt: Implement a bounded thread-safe queue (blocking put/take) and on top of it a fixed-size thread pool with submit()/execute(), shutdown() (drain) and shutdownNow() (interrupt). Variant: a client task scheduler with a cap on threads whose schedule() must return immediately without delaying clients.
lld.deliverable: Runnable code in a shared IDE using only mutex / condition variable / semaphore (ExecutorService, BlockingQueue, CountDownLatch disallowed)
probes: exception thrown inside a task — does it kill the worker?
per-task timeouts and cancellation
reclaiming idle threads / resizing the pool
shutdown vs shutdownNow semantics and thread interruption (catching InterruptedException alone was judged insufficient)
spurious wake-ups, full/empty signalling, fairness
what 'bounded queue of infinite size' means — clarify before coding
lld.evidence: 2026 India loop (bounded queue + executor, follow-ups on exceptions/timeouts/reclaiming), 2026 Bengaluru SDE-2 screen (shutdown/shutdownNow probed → Lean Hire), 2021 Bangalore screen (client scheduler), Dataford bank.

lld.title: Dependency-aware concurrent task / job scheduler (DAG execution)
lld.prompt: Tasks form a dependency graph; a task may start only when all parents finish. Either you are given get_next_jobs(finished_jobs) / a get_dependencies(task) API and a run(task) call, or the hierarchy itself. Execute everything with multiple worker threads as fast as possible. Variants: priority-based allocation and completion of tasks; workers fetching nodes from a utility function without starvation.
lld.deliverable: Working multithreaded code; discuss trade-offs, races and deadlocks
probes: in-degree tracking and signalling newly-ready tasks without busy-waiting
worker pool size, idle workers vs ready queue
detecting cycles / unsatisfiable dependencies and failed tasks
avoiding deadlock when workers wait on each other
starvation of low-priority or deep tasks
optimise: critical-path scheduling
lld.evidence: Most-reported Rubrik system-coding problem: L4 loop 2025 (get_next_jobs API), G5 Mar 2025 ('Strong Hire'), India May 2025, Bengaluru Sep 2024 (priority-based), Palo Alto 2021 (caused reject), Bengaluru 2021, Dataford bank.

lld.title: Concurrent list with searchers, inserters and deleters
lld.prompt: A singly-linked list (or generic structure) is used by three kinds of threads. Searchers only read and may run concurrently with each other. Inserters append at the tail: mutually exclusive with other inserters but may overlap any number of searchers. Deleters remove from anywhere: exclusive with everything (other deleters, inserters, searchers). Implement the synchronisation.
lld.deliverable: Thread-safe code using semaphores / read-write locks / condition variables; run it
probes: composition of a reader count, an insert mutex and a 'no-delete' gate
starvation of deleters under a steady stream of searchers — how to add writer preference
proving mutual-exclusion invariants
fairness vs throughput
what happens if a searcher is mid-traversal when a delete wants in
lld.evidence: Three reports within four months: SDE-2 (rejected, 2026-01), G6 Bangalore (rejected, 2026-02), Bangalore Rural Nov 2025 (starvation follow-up).

lld.title: Thread-safe one-dimensional parking lot (cars take 1 slot, trucks take 2 consecutive)
lld.prompt: Model a parking strip as a 1-D array of slots. Cars occupy one slot, trucks two adjacent slots. Many threads park and remove vehicles concurrently; implement park(vehicle) → position and leave(position) safely and efficiently.
lld.deliverable: Working concurrent code; discuss lock granularity
probes: finding two consecutive free slots without races (global lock vs per-slot locks vs free-run index)
fairness between trucks and cars — trucks starving when cars keep grabbing single slots
blocking vs returning failure when full; condition variables for waiters
fragmentation and compaction trade-offs
testing with concurrent arrivals
lld.evidence: 2026 India loop (redo round, paired with memory allocation) and 2026 SDE2 loop (round 2).

lld.title: Shared bathroom problem (Democrats / Republicans, capacity 3)
lld.prompt: A voting agency has one bathroom shared by Democrats and Republicans. Capacity is 3; occupants must all be from one party (3D, 2D, 1R ok; 2D+1R not). Each person takes f(name) seconds. People queue up; design the most efficient queue management so the most eligible waiting person enters as soon as there is room. Often preceded by a discussion of OS resource-allocation policies and their pros/cons.
lld.deliverable: Runnable multithreaded code (FIFO version at minimum), then discuss better policies
probes: FIFO vs party-batching vs priority and their starvation properties
condition variables per party vs one lock with predicates
ensuring the 'most eligible' rule under concurrent arrivals
how to prevent one party monopolising the room
mapping to classic readers-writers / unisex-bathroom problem
lld.evidence: G5 Selected loop (2024-05), Bengaluru Jun 2023, G5 Mar 2025 ('bathroom/Republican' round 2), recommended prep in a 2025 US report.

lld.title: Playground shared by one team at a time (max 10 players)
lld.prompt: A playground can be used by only one team at a time and holds at most 10 players concurrently. Players from different teams arrive simultaneously. Design the assignment so constraints hold; then discuss approaches that prevent any player from starving.
lld.deliverable: Concurrent code + starvation analysis
probes: team-switch policy (drain current team vs batch arrivals)
counting semaphore for capacity + team gate
starvation prevention: ticketing, turnstiles, bounded waiting
what if a team keeps arriving forever
lld.evidence: L4 loop 2025; a re-skin of the bathroom problem.

lld.title: Backup dependency graph with recovery chains and expiry
lld.prompt: Backups form a dependency graph (incrementals depend on earlier backups). Each backup has an end time and a retention period. Implement add_dependency(child, parent), find_recovery_chain(backup) (the ordered set needed to restore it) and expire_backups(now) (remove expired backups without breaking chains still needed). First single-threaded, then thread-safe. Variant: a backend that tracks backup lifecycle and execution dependencies under concurrent access.
lld.deliverable: Working code on HackerRank; thread-safe version expected within the hour
probes: graph representation and chain traversal
retention: can an expired parent be deleted if a live child depends on it?
lock granularity for concurrent add/expire/query
cycle prevention
complexity of expire over many backups
lld.evidence: G6 CPD loop 2026 (single-threaded done, ran out of time on thread safety → 'weak yes'); Dataford 'Backups and Dependencies System' (Hard).

lld.title: Changed-memory-block tracker with range merging (64-byte blocks)
lld.prompt: Design a thread-safe system that records which memory address blocks changed (block size 64 bytes). Writers report changed ranges like [1,2], [3,4], [6,9], [10,12]; a query must return merged ranges, e.g. [1,4] and [6,12]. Explain trade-offs between merge-on-write and merge-on-read.
lld.deliverable: Working implementation + thread-safety + trade-off discussion within 1 hour
probes: interval tree / ordered map for O(log n) insert with neighbour merging
concurrent writers vs readers: RW lock, snapshotting for consistent reads
block granularity → converting byte addresses to block ids
memory growth and compaction
how this maps to change-block tracking for incremental backup
lld.evidence: CPD loop Dec 2025 (candidate felt it went well); Dataford 'Memory Block Tracker with Thread Safety' (Hard).

lld.title: Logical memory unit / page cache with per-page history
lld.prompt: A CPU requests pages by pageId. If the page is in the logical memory unit return it, else fetch from physical memory and store it. Keep every entry ever recorded for a page and support 'most recent entry' and 'k most recent entries' for a given pageId. Then make it thread-safe.
lld.deliverable: Working code tested on several cases; thread-safe follow-up
probes: hash map keyed by pageId → linked list / deque of entries
eviction when the unit is full (LRU) and how history interacts with eviction
lock striping vs global lock
memory bound on history
lld.evidence: G5 loop 2025.

lld.title: Implement `cp` over a minimal file API, then parallelise it
lld.prompt: Given fopen(path) → fileId, fclose(fileId), read(fileId, offset) and write(fileId, offset) (fixed-size chunk per call), implement the Linux cp command. Follow-up: optimise copying from a slow floppy disk to a fast SSD. Variant: read/write a file by offset, then extend to multithreading.
lld.deliverable: Working code (first part ~25 min), then a multithreaded design — no ExecutorService/thread pools allowed
probes: chunked reads with multiple threads, assembling in order, bounded memory
coalescing writes to minimise expensive SSD writes
handling short reads/EOF, errors, partial failure and cleanup
thread count vs device parallelism; is the floppy even parallelisable?
syntax correctness under pressure — errors cost a Lean Hire
lld.evidence: Bengaluru SDE-2 (2026-02, Lean Hire) and G6 Bangalore (2026-02) reports.

lld.title: Bounded-memory data transfer / replication pipeline (one reader, many writers)
lld.prompt: Read data from a source and write it to a sink using one reader thread and multiple writer threads. Variants: replicate large binaries with limited memory; move thousands of 40 GB files across a 10 Gbps NIC while maximising utilisation.
lld.deliverable: Working concurrent code for the core pipeline, then throughput reasoning
probes: bounded buffer / chunk pool between reader and writers, backpressure
preserving chunk order at the sink vs positional writes
pipelining to keep the NIC saturated; number of parallel streams
checksums, retries and resumability
memory ceiling: chunk size × in-flight chunks
lld.evidence: Santa Clara Nov 2025 (reader/writers data transfer), US Oct 2025 (replicate large binaries, limited memory), Dataford (40 GB files over 10 Gbps).

lld.title: Two queues inside one fixed buffer / bounded buffer fed by two queues
lld.prompt: Given a single fixed-size buffer, implement two queues that share it as their only storage (no overflow while total usage fits). Variant: a bounded buffer that safely reads from two separate reader queues without exceeding memory. Then add concurrency.
lld.deliverable: Working code (Python accepted) in two parts: data structure, then concurrency primitives
probes: growing the queues from opposite ends vs dynamic partition
circular indexing and full/empty detection
condition variables for blocking enqueue/dequeue on each queue
fairness between the two sources; starvation
resizing / rebalancing the split
lld.evidence: Oct 2025 US report, India May 2025 loop, Dataford bank.

lld.title: Thread-safe (atomic) stack / queue with a custom lock, O(1) operations
lld.prompt: Implement a linked-list stack (or queue) with O(1) push/pop that is safe under many threads — first with your own lock, then discuss a lock-free CAS version. Similar in spirit to Design Bounded Blocking Queue.
lld.deliverable: Runnable code + follow-ups on primitives
probes: mutex + condvar vs spinlock vs CAS
ABA problem and memory reclamation in lock-free stacks
blocking pop on empty vs returning failure
memory ordering / visibility
which concurrency primitives exist in your language and how they are implemented
lld.evidence: Palo Alto 2021 onsite, US Aug 2025 screen ('atomic stack'), US Oct 2025 onsite ('atomic queue with custom lock'), Dataford.

lld.title: Scheduled executor / asynchronous notification scheduler
lld.prompt: Implement schedule(task, delay), scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period) and scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, initialDelay, delay) on a fixed set of worker threads. Variants: an asynchronous notification scheduler; a calendar-invite sender that sleeps and wakes using a priority queue.
lld.deliverable: Working code with a min-heap of next-run times and timed condition-variable waits
probes: fixed-rate vs fixed-delay semantics and drift
waking the scheduler early when a sooner task is added
cancellation and shutdown while tasks are sleeping
long-running task blocking periodic ones; thread count
clock source and spurious wake-ups
lld.round: System coding (screen for senior; onsite for SWE)
lld.evidence: Senior screen 2021 (ScheduledExecutorService), Palo Alto 2021 (calendar sender), US Oct 2025 onsite (async notification scheduler).

lld.title: Multi-node task manager with rebalancing
lld.prompt: There are N worker nodes. Implement runTask() (execute a task on a node), AddTask(nodeId, taskId), rebalanceTask() (move tasks away from a node overloaded with CPU-intensive tasks) and printTask() (pending tasks per node).
lld.deliverable: Class design + working code; per-node queues and a rebalancing policy
probes: rebalance criterion: pending count vs CPU weight; target = average load
moving tasks safely while workers consume (locking per node)
avoiding ping-pong rebalancing
complexity of rebalance

lld.title: Concurrent ticket / seat booking (BookMyShow-like)
lld.prompt: Implement seat reservation for shows where many users book concurrently; no double-booking, bookings of multiple seats are atomic.
lld.deliverable: Runnable Java/C++ with proper synchronisation (Rubrik's platform runs multithreaded code)
probes: choice of primitive — the interviewer closely examined CyclicBarrier vs Semaphore vs locks
lock per seat vs per show, deadlock-free multi-seat locking (ordered acquisition)
exception handling and rollback of partial bookings
a one-line bug let multiple threads into the critical section — be able to reason about your own race
lld.evidence: G5 loop 2025 (positive feedback after a ~20-minute debugging detour).

lld.title: Design and implement an in-memory Linux-like file system
lld.prompt: Open-ended: design the classes and implement a file system supporting directories and files (mkdir, create/write/read, ls, path resolution), delivered in 3–4 incremental parts with two interviewers. Pointer variant to prepare: add snapshots.
lld.deliverable: Working code for as many parts as possible; final 10 minutes Q&A
probes: tree of inodes vs path→node map
path normalisation and error cases
snapshots via copy-on-write (if asked)
concurrency on shared directories
lld.round: Design/coding round with two interviewers (60 min)
lld.evidence: New-grad loop Sept 2025 (3 parts done, 4th partial). Compare LC 588 Design In-Memory File System.

lld.title: Versioned in-memory key-value store with snapshots
lld.prompt: Implement get(key), put(key, value), take_snapshot() → snapshotId and get_from_snapshot(snapshotId, key) with time-versioned history.
lld.deliverable: Working code; discuss memory growth
probes: per-key version lists + binary search (Snapshot Array generalised)
snapshot cost O(1) vs copying
garbage-collecting old snapshots
thread safety of put vs snapshot
lld.evidence: Dataford bank; Snapshot Array itself was asked as system coding in 2025.

lld.title: Text editor: insert(offset, text), delete(offset, length), getContents()
lld.prompt: Design the interface and implementation of a text editor with the three operations; pick a data structure that keeps edits efficient and justify it.
lld.deliverable: Clean OO code judged on quality and complexity within a strict 45 minutes
probes: string vs rope vs gap buffer vs piece table
complexity of each op
undo as a follow-up
implement a simpler version first rather than leave methods empty
lld.evidence: On-campus SDE intern loop (GfG, 2021).

lld.title: Rate limiter implementation
lld.prompt: Implement a thread-safe rate limiter (token bucket / sliding window) for many clients.
lld.deliverable: Working concurrent code
probes: per-client state and memory
lock contention under many clients
clock handling and burst behaviour
distributed extension
lld.evidence: Senior SDE onsite summary on 1point3acres (login-gated) lists 'rate limiter implementation' in system coding; also commonly cited in prep articles.

lld.title: Producer–consumer from primitives (and dining philosophers)
lld.prompt: Implement a multi-producer multi-consumer bounded buffer with mutex and condition variables (no BlockingQueue); be ready to do the same style of reasoning for dining philosophers and reader–writer.
lld.deliverable: Runnable code; explain every wait/notify
probes: lost wake-ups, notify vs notifyAll
deadlock avoidance (ordered acquisition, resource hierarchy)
fairness and starvation
how BlockingQueue / ConcurrentHashMap are implemented internally
lld.evidence: Bengaluru 2021 loop; Blind threads name producer-consumer, reader-writer and dining philosophers as the core prep set; Medium prep guide.

lld.title: Debugging round: multithreaded barber-shop simulation
lld.prompt: You receive ~170–180 lines simulating a barber shop: customers, a chair, shared tools (brush, scissors, comb) and several threads. Multiple bugs are planted (missing synchronisation, logic errors) and the program deadlocks at shutdown (e.g. 21 customers arrive, 18 served, 3 stuck → TLE). Explain the code, fix every bug so all tests pass, then suggest improvements.
lld.deliverable: Fully working program by end of round; partial fixes earned 'weak yes' + 'no' → reject
probes: trace the shutdown path for threads waiting forever
identify unprotected shared state
explain why each fix is correct
improvement suggestions must themselves be correct
lld.evidence: G6 CPD loop 2026.

lld.title: Debugging round: producer–consumer code with missing synchronisation
lld.prompt: A producer–consumer program (C++ or Java; one version split across Producer, Consumer, Queue, ProducerMessageGenerator, ConsumerMessageGenerator classes) has unprotected critical sections, race conditions and several logic/design flaws. Find and fix all of them within the round; one variant required running code within 50 minutes.
lld.deliverable: Compiling, passing program; interviewers stated they expected a fully working solution
probes: where the critical section is unprotected
deadlock vs livelock vs lost wake-up
fixing a deadlock without introducing a compile error (one candidate failed exactly this)
design flaws beyond synchronisation (ownership, shutdown)
lld.evidence: G5 loop 2025 (C++, found after a hint), CPD Dec 2025 (5 classes, ran out of time), new-grad Sept 2025 (50 min, compile error), Dataford.

lld.title: Debugging round: concurrent banking application
lld.prompt: A banking app runs transfers/deposits across multiple threads. Understand and explain the code, find the bugs (races on balances, deadlock on two-account transfers, lock contention / high latency), fix them, and propose multithreaded optimisations.
lld.deliverable: Explain + fix + suggest (read–write lock, concurrent hash map, ordered lock acquisition)
probes: ordered locking for transfers between two accounts
coarse vs fine-grained locks and their latency impact
which operations can proceed concurrently (reads)
what goes wrong under concurrent execution of each function
lld.evidence: Pune CPD Sept 2024; Dataford 'debug a multithreaded banking application'.

lld.title: Implement three methods of a given class (then make it fast under threads)
lld.prompt: A class skeleton is provided; implement three of its methods using appropriate data structures (two were completed in 60 minutes by the reporter). Follow-up: how would you improve performance in a multithreaded environment?
lld.deliverable: Complete working code
probes: data-structure choice per method
contention hot spots and lock striping
finishing all methods in time
lld.evidence: Pune CPD Sept 2024 (rejected after debugging round).

lld.title: Reader–writer lock from scratch
lld.prompt: Implement a read–write lock (acquireRead/releaseRead/acquireWrite/releaseWrite) using a mutex and condition variables, and handle the edge cases.
lld.deliverable: Correct implementation; the 2026 reporter struggled and was given a redo round
probes: writer starvation and writer-preference variants
reentrancy and lock upgrade/downgrade
fairness (ticket-based)
spurious wake-ups and notifyAll cost
lld.evidence: 2026 India loop (round 2 'did not go well', redo granted).
